text: Gertrude Katherine Lathrop (December 24, 1896–March 16, 1986) was an American sculptor renowned for her medallion work and sculptures of small animals. She was born in Albany, New York, to artist Ida Pulis Lathrop and Cyrus Clark Lathrop, and her sister Dorothy P. Lathrop was also an artist. Lathrop studied at the Art Students League in 1918 and at the School of American Sculpture, both under Gutzon Borglum. Her first exhibition was at the National Academy of Design in 1921. In 1924, she traveled to Gloucester, Massachusetts to study with Charles Grafly. She received an Honorable Mention from the Art Institute of Chicago in 1924, as well as the Helen Foster Barnett prize and the National Academy of Design award in 1928. In 1936, she designed the Albany Charter half dollar, and in 1938, she was commissioned by the Westchester County Coin Club of New Rochelle, New York, to design the New Rochelle 250th Anniversary half dollar. In 1964, she was awarded the Allied Artists of America's Medal of Honor; in 1967, she received the Pen and Brush Club's silver medal; and in 1970, she won the John Sanford Saltus Gold Medal from the British Numismatic Society. Lathrop was skilled in medal design and portrait modeling, but her primary passion was sculpting animals, a choice she explained by stating, "I chose to model animals because of their infinite variety of form and texture and their great beauty, for even the lowliest of them have beauty, yes even the ward bug, with his magnificent tusks." In 1954, she moved to Falls Village, Connecticut with her sister, a noted illustrator of children's books, where she resided for the rest of her life. Her works are held in the collections of the Seattle Art Museum, the Smithsonian American Art Museum, the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the Albany Institute of History & Art, and the Metropolitan Museum of Art. She died in Falls Village, Connecticut in 1986.
